original_value: Differential privacy has become one of the widely used mechanisms for protecting sensitive information in databases and information systems. Although differential privacy provides a clear measure of privacy guarantee, it implicitly assumes that each individual corresponds to a single record in the result of a database query. This assumption may not hold in many database query applications. When an individual has multiple records, strict implementation of differential privacy may cause significant information loss. In this study, we extend the differential privacy principle to situations where multiple records in a database are associated with the same individual. We propose a new privacy principle that integrates differential privacy with the Pareto principle in analyzing privacy risk and data utility. When applied to the situations with multiple records per person, the proposed approach can significantly reduce the information loss in the released query results with a relatively small relaxation in the differential privacy guarantee. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is evaluated using three real-world databases.

result.paraphrase: Differential privacy is now one of the most widely used methods for safeguarding sensitive data in databases and information systems. While it offers a clear privacy guarantee, it implicitly assumes that each person corresponds to a single record in a database query result, an assumption that does not hold in many query applications. If one individual has multiple records, strict enforcement of differential privacy can lead to substantial information loss. In this study, we extend the differential privacy principle to cases where multiple database records are linked to the same individual. We introduce a new privacy principle that combines differential privacy and the Pareto principle to analyze privacy risk and data utility. Applied to scenarios with multiple records per person, this approach can markedly reduce information loss in released query results while only slightly relaxing the differential privacy guarantee. Its effectiveness is assessed using three real-world databases.
